stem: Jonas leaves `sketch.txt` in the shared `/tmp`, and Ada tries to delete it. The directory shows `drwxrwxrwt`. Why does `rm` fail?
explanation: On a world-writable directory, the sticky bit restricts deleting and renaming to the file’s owner, the directory’s owner and root.

options.text: The `t` marks the directory as read-only, so nobody can delete anything.
options.rationale: The `t` does not remove write permission; the directory stays writable.

options.text: The sticky bit (`t`) lets only the file’s owner, the directory’s owner or root delete files there.
options.rationale: With the sticky bit, write permission on the directory no longer lets everybody delete other users’ files.

options.text: The `t` means the directory is cleared at every reboot, so deleting is pointless.
options.rationale: The `t` concerns deletion rights, not clean-up at boot.

options.text: Others have no execute permission on the directory, so Ada cannot reach the file.
options.rationale: The final `t` includes execute for others.

stem: What does the `t` at the end of `drwxrwxrwt` tell you?
explanation: A capital `T` would mean sticky without execute for others. The octal mode is `1777`.

options.text: The directory is temporary and will be removed.
options.rationale: Nothing in the mode marks removal.

options.text: The directory is a symbolic link to a target.
options.rationale: Links show `l` as the first character.

options.text: Others can only traverse it, not write.
options.rationale: The write bit for others is still shown as `w`.

options.text: The sticky bit is set and others also have execute permission.
options.rationale: A lower-case `t` is the sticky bit on top of `x` for others.

stem: Mira wants a scratch place for files that survive a reboot. Which directory is meant for that?
explanation: Both `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` are writable by everyone with the sticky bit. `/var/tmp` keeps data longer.

options.text: `/var/tmp`
options.rationale: Files in `/var/tmp` are expected to be preserved between reboots.

options.text: `/tmp`
options.rationale: Programs must assume `/tmp` is cleared at boot or earlier.

options.text: `/proc`
options.rationale: This is a virtual file system for kernel information.

options.text: `/dev/shm`
options.rationale: This is shared memory that disappears when the machine stops.

stem: Mira creates `/srv/uploads` for the whole team and wants each person to delete only their own files there. Which command sets that up?
explanation: The sticky bit is the fourth digit in front of the usual three. `chmod +t DIR` sets it too.

options.text: `chmod 0777 /srv/uploads`
options.rationale: Everyone could delete everybody else’s files.

options.text: `chmod 4777 /srv/uploads`
options.rationale: The leading `4` is set-user-ID, not the sticky bit.

options.text: `chmod 1777 /srv/uploads`
options.rationale: The leading `1` is the sticky bit, plus rwx for everyone.

options.text: `chmod 1700 /srv/uploads`
options.rationale: This sets the sticky bit but locks everyone else out.

stem: What happens to the symbolic link `latest.tar` when its target `pixel-raiders-1.1.tar` is deleted?
explanation: A symbolic link holds a path. Removing the link with `rm` leaves the target untouched, but removing the target leaves a dangling link.

options.text: The link is deleted too.
options.rationale: The system does not track links.

options.text: The link becomes a regular file with a copy of the content.
options.rationale: No copy of the data exists.

options.text: The link stays but is dangling: opening it gives "No such file or directory".
options.rationale: A symlink only stores a path; it does not keep the target alive.

options.text: The link points to the trash.
options.rationale: Linux has no automatic trash for this.

stem: Which statement describes a symbolic link correctly?
explanation: Symbolic links can point to directories and across file systems. Hard links cannot.

options.text: It is a small file that holds the path to another file or directory.
options.rationale: Following the link means looking up that path.

options.text: It is a second name for the same data on disk, sharing its inode.
options.rationale: That describes a hard link.

options.text: It is a copy of the target that updates itself.
options.rationale: No copy is made.

options.text: It can only point to files on the same file system.
options.rationale: Symlinks can cross file systems.

stem: Which command makes `latest.tar` a symbolic link pointing to `pixel-raiders-1.1.tar`?
explanation: `ln -s TARGET LINKNAME` creates a symbolic link; the order is like `cp`: existing thing first.

options.text: `ln -s latest.tar pixel-raiders-1.1.tar`
options.rationale: This creates a link called `pixel-raiders-1.1.tar` pointing at `latest.tar`.

options.text: `ln pixel-raiders-1.1.tar latest.tar`
options.rationale: Without `-s` this creates a hard link.

options.text: `ls -s pixel-raiders-1.1.tar latest.tar`
options.rationale: `ls` lists files and does not create links.

options.text: `ln -s pixel-raiders-1.1.tar latest.tar`
options.rationale: The target comes first, then the link name.

stem: Which statements about `/tmp` are true? (Choose TWO.)
explanation: `/tmp` is shared scratch space: world-writable with the sticky bit.

options.text: Every user may create files there.
options.rationale: The directory is world-writable.

options.text: The sticky bit stops users from deleting each other’s files.
options.rationale: That is the purpose of the `t` bit.

options.text: Only root may write there.
options.rationale: Mode 1777 grants write to all.

options.text: Its files are kept forever and never cleaned.
options.rationale: They may be removed at boot or by cleanup jobs.

options.text: The sticky bit hides the files of other users.
options.rationale: It restricts deleting, not listing.

stem: Which statements about symbolic links are true? (Choose TWO.)
explanation: A symbolic link is a pointer. Deleting it never affects the target.

options.text: Removing the link with `rm` leaves the target unchanged.
options.rationale: `rm` deletes the link only.

options.text: They share the inode of their target.
options.rationale: That describes a hard link.

options.text: They keep working after the target is deleted.
options.rationale: They dangle.

options.text: They cannot cross file systems.
options.rationale: They can.

options.text: They can point to a directory.
options.rationale: The target may be any path.

stem: Type the command that makes `builds/latest.tar` a symbolic link to `pixel-raiders-1.1.tar` (the link target is given relative to the link’s directory).
explanation: `ln -s TARGET LINK`; a relative target is resolved from the link’s directory.

stem: What is true about the directory `/run`?
explanation: `/run` holds runtime data such as PID files and sockets. It lives in memory and starts empty at every boot. `/var/run` is a link to it.

options.text: It is the place for files that must survive a reboot.
options.rationale: That describes `/var/tmp`.

options.text: It stores the home directories of the system users.
options.rationale: Those are in `/home` or elsewhere.

options.text: It holds runtime data such as PID files, and is empty after a boot.
options.rationale: It is a memory-backed tmpfs.

options.text: It is a link to `/tmp` for all users.
options.rationale: `/var/run` is a link to `/run`, not the other way round.

stem: Mira creates a relative symbolic link from another directory with `-r`. What does `readlink` print?
explanation: `ln -rs` works out the path from the link's own directory, so the target is stored as `../docs`.
command: cd ~ && mkdir -p proj/docs proj/bin && ln -rs proj/docs proj/bin/docs && readlink proj/bin/docs

stem: Mira is in `/home/mira/proj/` and wants `bin/docs` to point at `docs` in the same folder as `bin`. Which command lets `ln` work out the relative path for her?
explanation: `-r` makes the link target relative to the link's location, so it is stored as `../docs`.

options.text: `ln -rs docs bin/docs`
options.rationale: With `-r`, ln computes the relative target.

options.text: `ln -s -p docs bin/docs`
options.rationale: `-p` is not an option of `ln` that does this.

options.text: `ln -h docs bin/docs`
options.rationale: `-h` does not create a relative link.

options.text: `ln docs bin/docs`
options.rationale: Without `-s` it is a hard link, which can't point at a directory.
